lead: Every property of moist air comes from two measured numbers: the dry-bulb temperature and the amount of water vapour. Absolute humidity Y is the mass of vapour per kg of dry air; relative humidity compares the vapour pressure to the saturation value; the dew point is where saturation begins. Engineers use these numbers to size cooling towers, dryers, air-conditioning ducts and humidifiers, where the water content decides how much heat and water the air can carry.
prereq: You need: school-level vapour pressure and the gas laws, and the pure-water steam tables for saturation pressures and latent heats.

blocks.text: Moist air is a mixture of dry air and water vapour. The dry air never changes as humidity changes, so we count water against dry air. Absolute humidity (also called humidity ratio) Y is the mass of water vapour carried by 1 kg of dry air. It is a pure number in kg water per kg dry air.

blocks.where: Y is the absolute humidity in kg water/kg dry air; p_A is the partial pressure of water vapour in kPa; P is the total pressure in kPa; 0.622 = 18.02/28.97, the ratio of the molar mass of water to that of air.

blocks.text: The same ratio comes from Dalton's law. The vapour and the air fill the same volume at the same temperature, so the mole ratio equals the pressure ratio. The number 0.622 converts that mole ratio into a mass ratio.

At a given temperature there is a maximum vapour pressure the air can hold: the saturation pressure p_AS, read from steam tables. The humidity at that maximum is the saturation humidity Y_s, obtained by putting p_AS in place of p_A.

blocks.where: Y_s is the saturation humidity in kg water/kg dry air at that temperature; p_AS is the vapour pressure of water at that temperature in kPa.

blocks.text: Relative humidity (RH) is a percentage. It compares the actual vapour pressure with the saturation pressure at the same temperature.

blocks.where: RH is the relative humidity in per cent; p_A is the actual vapour pressure in kPa; p_AS is the saturation pressure at the same dry-bulb temperature in kPa.

blocks.text: Percentage humidity (percentage saturation) compares humidities instead of pressures: 100 Y/Y_s at the same temperature. The two numbers are close when the air is nearly saturated and drift apart as the air dries, because Y is not linear in p_A. An examiner who writes RH when the calculation needs percentage humidity changes the answer.

Saturation pressure rises fast with temperature: at 40 °C it is 7.38 kPa, at 12.7 °C about 1.48 kPa. So warm air at a fixed Y always shows a lower RH, which is why a room feels dry on a hot afternoon.

Dew point is the temperature at which the vapour present just saturates the air at constant pressure. Below it, water condenses as dew or fog. To find it, take the actual p_A and look up the saturation temperature of water at that pressure.

Dew point is fixed by Y and P alone, not by the dry-bulb temperature. Two air samples with the same Y share one dew point. That is why dew point is a comfort measure in weather reports: air at 30 °C and 40 % RH feels sticky in Chennai because its dew point is near 16 °C, high enough to stop sweat evaporating.
Air below 0 °C has a frost point instead of a dew point. Only a few universities teach this chapter on its own; most fold it into the psychrometric chart, covered in 7.2.
Humid volume v_H is the volume occupied by 1 kg of dry air plus its vapour, in m³/kg dry air. Treat the mixture as ideal and use the molar volume 22.414 m³/kmol at 0 °C and 101.3 kPa.

blocks.where: v_H is the humid volume in m³/kg dry air; Y is the absolute humidity; T is the absolute temperature in K; 28.97 and 18.02 are the molar masses of air and water in kg/kmol.

blocks.text: Humid heat c_s is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of dry air plus its vapour by 1 K. The two specific heats 1.005 and 1.88 kJ/(kg·K) belong to dry air and to water vapour.

blocks.where: c_s is the humid heat in kJ/(kg dry air·K); Y is the absolute humidity in kg/kg dry air; 1.005 and 1.88 are the specific heats of dry air and water vapour in kJ/(kg·K).

blocks.text: Enthalpy H of moist air is measured above a reference of dry air and liquid water at 0 °C. It has a sensible part for warming the mixture and a latent part for the vapour already formed. The latent heat of water at 0 °C is taken as 2500 kJ/kg.

blocks.where: H is the enthalpy in kJ/kg dry air; T is the dry-bulb temperature in °C; T_ref = 0 °C; λ_ref = 2500 kJ/kg, the latent heat of vaporisation of water at the reference temperature.

blocks.text: These definitions feed directly into 7.3 and into cooling-tower heat balances in 7.5.

figure.caption: Start from dry-bulb temperature and relative humidity, read the saturation pressure, and compute downwards to enthalpy. The same chain is followed in the worked example: 40 °C and 20 % give Y = 0.0092 and H = 63.9 kJ/kg dry air.

spec.title: From two measured numbers to air properties
spec.aria: A five-step downward chain from dry-bulb temperature and relative humidity through vapour pressure and humidity to humid volume, humid heat and enthalpy.

examples.question: Air at 40 °C and 20 % relative humidity flows at 101.3 kPa. The saturation pressure of water at 40 °C is 7.38 kPa. Find (a) the partial pressure of water vapour, (b) the absolute humidity, (c) the dew point, (d) the humid volume, (e) the humid heat and (f) the enthalpy above 0 °C.
steps: (a) Partial pressure: p_A = RH × p_AS = 0.20 × 7.38 = 1.476 kPa, say 1.48 kPa.
(c) Dew point: find the saturation temperature at p_A = 1.48 kPa. From steam tables this is about 12.7 °C. The air begins to condense water below that temperature.
examples.answer: p_A = 1.48 kPa, Y = 0.00922 kg/kg dry air, dew point ≈ 12.7 °C, v_H = 0.90 m³/kg dry air, c_s = 1.022 kJ/(kg·K) and H = 63.9 kJ/kg dry air.
examples.check:
T = 40.0
RH = 0.20
P = 101.3
pAS = 7.38
pA = RH * pAS
Y = 0.622 * pA / (P - pA)
vH = (1/28.97 + Y/18.02) * 22.414 * ((T + 273.15)/273.15)
cs = 1.005 + 1.88 * Y
H = cs * T + Y * 2500
print(round(pA, 2))
print(round(Y, 5))
print(round(vH, 2))
print(round(cs, 3))
print(round(H, 1))

traps: Reading relative humidity as the water content: at the same Y, warmer air has a lower RH, so 20 % RH at 40 °C holds more water than 20 % RH at 20 °C.
Using percentage humidity and relative humidity interchangeably. They are equal only at saturation, and differ noticeably for dry air.
Putting p_A in the denominator of the humidity formula as P + p_A, or using P = 1 atm without converting to the kPa of the steam tables.
Forgetting the dry-air basis: the humid heat and enthalpy are per kg dry air, not per kg of moist air.
Mixing dew point with wet-bulb temperature: wet-bulb is an adiabatic saturation value, dew point is a saturation-from-vapour-pressure value, and they coincide only at 100 % RH.

quiz.q: Define absolute humidity and give its units.
quiz.a: Absolute humidity Y is the mass of water vapour carried by unit mass of dry air: Y = 0.622 p_A/(P − p_A), in kg water/kg dry air.

quiz.q: Why does the same absolute humidity give a lower relative humidity at 40 °C than at 20 °C?
quiz.a: RH = 100 p_A/p_AS. For a fixed Y, p_A is fixed. p_AS rises steeply with temperature, so at 40 °C the denominator is much larger and RH falls.

quiz.q: Air at 30 °C and 50 % RH is at 101.3 kPa; p_AS at 30 °C is 4.24 kPa. Find p_A and Y.
For Y = 0.0133 kg/kg dry air at 30 °C, find the humid heat and enthalpy above 0 °C.
Two rooms hold air at the same dew point but different dry-bulb temperatures. Compare their Y and their RH.
quiz.a: Same dew point means the same p_A and therefore the same Y. The room at the higher dry-bulb temperature has the larger saturation pressure, so its RH is lower. Their enthalpies differ because the sensible term c_s T differs.

quiz.q: An examiner says percentage humidity equals relative humidity. Give a case where the error is large.
quiz.a: At low humidity the two diverge. Example: p_A = 1.48 kPa, P = 101.3 kPa gives Y = 0.00922. If p_AS = 7.38 kPa, Y_s = 0.622 × 7.38/93.92 = 0.0489, so percentage humidity = 100 × 0.00922/0.0489 = 18.9 %, against RH = 20 %. The gap grows as the air dries.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real design software carries the humidity functions as fitted equations, most often the Hyland–Wexler or ASHRAE formulations, so that p_AS is computed without a table lookup at any temperature. Air-conditioning practice adds the concept of a moist-air enthalpy that includes the liquid water carried as droplets. Research on drying of food and pharmaceuticals couples these air properties to heat and mass transfer inside the solid. Search terms to follow: psychrometric equations, ASHRAE fundamentals, dew-point hygrometers, and enthalpy of moist air.
